tips.title: For a common illness, start at primary care; know your scheme's referral rule before you go to a bigger hospital
tips.cost: Under PM-JAY the listed package is cashless for an eligible beneficiary. ESIC and CGHS have their own contribution and rate rules. A hospital that is not empanelled for your scheme will bill you.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no single insurance deductible that accumulates across hospital levels. What you pay depends on your scheme. Under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, an eligible family gets cashless cover of up to ₹5 lakh a year for secondary and tertiary hospital care at an empanelled hospital, with no deductible and no co-payment for the listed packages. ESIC, CGHS and the state schemes have their own rules. Starting at a primary health centre, an urban primary health centre or a family doctor is still the sensible first step: it is cheaper and faster for a simple problem, and it produces a referral if you need one.
tips.benefit: PM-JAY is run by the National Health Authority and pays an empanelled hospital a package rate for a listed procedure, so the eligible patient does not pay the bill at the counter. ESIC covers insured workers and their families through its own dispensaries and hospitals, with referral to tie-up hospitals for specialist care. CGHS covers central government employees and pensioners through wellness centres, and a referral from the wellness centre is normally needed before treatment at a private empanelled hospital, except in an emergency. A state scheme may add its own cover. Ask at the hospital's Ayushman desk or at your scheme's office which package applies, before you are admitted.
tips.sources: National Health Authority, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Central Government Health Scheme. <https://cghs.nic.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A package covers a defined procedure, not every cost: a non-listed investigation, an implant or a room upgrade may sit outside it. A private hospital that is not empanelled for your scheme will bill you in full. Do not assume a government hospital is free; some charge user fees. If you are treated in another state, check whether your scheme allows it before you travel. Keep the referral paper and the package authorisation with your discharge summary.

tips.title: There is no uniform "lower hospital, higher reimbursement" ladder in India — what you pay depends on the scheme and the hospital's empanelment
tips.cost: A scheme patient pays nothing for a covered package; a self-paying patient pays the hospital's bill. Ask for the estimate in writing before admission either way.
tips.inPlainWords: Some insurance systems reimburse a higher share at a lower-level hospital and a lower share at a big one. India's public schemes do not work that way. PM-JAY pays a package rate set by the scheme for a listed procedure at an empanelled hospital. ESIC and CGHS have their own rates and referral rules. A private hospital's bill for the same operation can be several times a government hospital's. The useful comparison is not the hospital's "level" but whether the procedure is covered and whether the hospital is empanelled.
tips.benefit: Under PM-JAY the empanelled hospital is paid the package rate for the procedure, and the eligible beneficiary pays nothing for it; the rate is set by the scheme, not by the hospital's size. Under CGHS the rates are fixed by the scheme for listed procedures, and treatment at a private hospital normally follows a referral from a wellness centre. Under ESIC, treatment is through the ESIC network. For a patient paying out of pocket, a government hospital, a government medical college or a district hospital is usually far cheaper than a private one for the same procedure.
tips.sources: National Health Authority, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Central Government Health Scheme. <https://cghs.nic.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Do not choose a hospital by its name. Check whether it is empanelled for your scheme and for the procedure, and ask for the package name and the estimate in writing. A "free" package may exclude implants, consumables, a private room or follow-up. For a planned operation, compare the package with the out-of-pocket cost at a government hospital. If you are paying yourself, ask for the itemised estimate before you are admitted.

tips.title: Go to a major hospital via a referral from a local clinic or the hospital’s referral center — don’t turn to scalpers.
tips.cost: No direct cost, but an extra referral step is required.
tips.inPlainWords: Major hospitals must set aside a portion of appointments and beds specifically for patients referred from local clinics. They must also establish a referral center or designate a dedicated department to handle referrals — this requirement will be fully implemented by 2027. Not being able to book a slot online does not mean there is no way in. Scalpers charge exorbitant fees and may even route you to the wrong department.
tips.benefit: Lead hospitals in tightly integrated medical networks must reserve a specific share of appointments and beds for patients referred from local clinics, and promptly admit them. Such networks consist of multiple hospitals and community health centers working together. In other words, there is a separate pool of appointments and beds reserved for referred patients, separate from the general booking pool. All hospitals must set up referral centers or assign a dedicated department by 2027.
tips.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Authority. <https://nha.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The reserved appointments and beds are specifically meant for referred patients. Failing to book online does not mean there is no way in. Using scalpers is not only costly but may also lead to being assigned to the wrong department. If you cannot locate the referral center, call the hospital’s service line for help.

tips.title: Before you travel to another state or city for treatment, check whether your scheme covers it there
tips.cost: A covered package is cashless; the travel, stay and any non-package item are yours. A self-paying patient pays the metro private hospital's bill.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no home-province insurance boundary that requires a senior doctor's approval before you can be treated elsewhere. What matters is your scheme. Under PM-JAY an eligible beneficiary can use an empanelled hospital in another state, because the scheme is portable. Under CGHS, treatment outside your registered city normally needs the local wellness centre's permission, except in an emergency. Under ESIC the referral is within the ESIC network. Ask the scheme's office before you travel, not after.
tips.benefit: PM-JAY is a national scheme, and a beneficiary can seek care at an empanelled hospital in another state; the hospital claims from the scheme through its state implementation. CGHS beneficiaries are attached to a wellness centre in their city, and a referral from that centre is the normal route to a specialist or a private empanelled hospital; a beneficiary who moves city can apply to change the attachment. ESIC insured persons are treated at the dispensary or hospital to which they are attached, with referral for specialist care. The details differ by scheme and state, so the scheme's own office is the authority.
tips.sources: National Health Authority, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Central Government Health Scheme. <https://cghs.nic.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Keep the referral or the authorisation with the discharge summary; without it a claim can be refused even for necessary treatment. An emergency is treated first and regularised afterwards, but that is not a reason to skip the paperwork on a planned trip. If you are paying yourself, the cost in a metro private hospital can be far higher than at home, and the scheme's package, if any, will not cover travel and stay. Ask for the estimate in writing before you go.

tips.title: Do not use a tertiary hospital only to refill a prescription — a stable chronic condition can be followed up in primary care
tips.cost: A primary health centre or wellness centre visit is free or low cost. A tertiary hospital's outpatient fee, travel and waiting time are the hidden cost of the repeat visit.
tips.inPlainWords: There is no Indian rule that a prescription for a stable chronic disease lasts twelve weeks. A registered doctor prescribes for the period he or she thinks clinically appropriate, and a medicine on the schedule that requires a prescription cannot be sold without one. What you can do is stop using a big hospital's outpatient department only to collect a repeat prescription. A primary health centre, an urban primary health centre, a polyclinic or your family doctor can monitor blood pressure, sugar or thyroid, renew the prescription, and refer you back if something changes.
tips.benefit: The Ayushman Bharat network of health and wellness centres and primary health centres is designed for exactly this: routine follow-up, medicine refills and screening close to home. A family doctor who knows your history can adjust a dose and spot a change sooner than a new registrar at a big hospital. The big hospital's outpatient slot is better spent on the problem that needs it. Continuity also means fewer duplicate tests, because the same clinician sees the trend rather than a single reading.
tips.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; National Health Authority, Ayushman Bharat health and wellness centres. <https://nha.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A stable condition can become unstable, and a primary-care doctor should send you back if the readings, the symptoms or the tests change. Do not extend a prescription indefinitely without a review; the dose and the medicine need checking. Some medicines, and some conditions, need a specialist's supervision, and a refill at primary level is not a substitute. Keep a written list of your medicines, doses and last test results, and take it to every visit.

tips.title: If you doubt the treatment, ask for a certified copy of the records in writing — India has no statutory "sealing" ceremony, but you can preserve the evidence
tips.cost: A certified copy usually carries a copying fee. A lawyer's notice is not needed for the first request.
tips.inPlainWords: India does not have the procedure, used in some countries, of sealing the medical file on the spot with both sides present. What you have is a right of access. The Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 provides for the registration and regulation of clinical establishments, and the state rules made under it require a medical record to be kept. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 a patient is the data principal and can ask the hospital, as data fiduciary, for a copy of the personal data it holds. Put the request in writing, keep the acknowledgement, and ask for a certified copy.
tips.benefit: The Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 and the state rules framed under it set out what a medical record must contain and how long it is kept. The Charter of Patients' Rights, 2019 states the patient's right to information about the treatment and to the medical record. The DPDP Act, 2023 gives a data principal the right to access a copy of personal data and to correction or erasure, subject to the Act's conditions. If a dispute reaches a consumer commission or a court, the hospital can be required to produce the record, and the BNSS, 2023 gives the police and the court powers to seize evidence in a criminal case.
tips.sources: Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Charter of Patients' Rights. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Never take the only copy; ask for a certified copy and leave the original in the hospital's custody. If you suspect that a drip, a transfusion, an injection or a medicine caused harm, ask the hospital in writing to preserve the bag, vial, syringe and packaging, and note the batch number and the time. India has no joint-sealing rule, so your written request is the protection. If the hospital refuses, complain to the state authority that registers clinical establishments, and take the refusal to the consumer commission or the court with the rest of your file.

tips.title: After every visit, keep your own copy of the records, the test reports and the scans
tips.cost: A copying fee, usually modest. The habit costs a folder and ten minutes.
tips.inPlainWords: You are entitled to a copy of your medical record. In India a clinical establishment must maintain records, and the patient can ask for a copy; the Charter of Patients' Rights, 2019 lists access to records among the patient's rights, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 gives you a right to a copy of the personal data a hospital holds about you. Ask at the records counter, in writing, and keep the copy: it is what a new doctor, an insurer or a consumer commission will ask for.
tips.benefit: The documents to collect are the outpatient card, the discharge summary, the operation note, the anaesthesia record, the laboratory and imaging reports, the histopathology report and the itemised bill. They prove what was done and when, which is what a second opinion, an insurance claim or a negligence complaint turns on. A hospital can charge a reasonable copying fee. The DPDP Act, 2023 makes the hospital a data fiduciary with an obligation to keep the data accurate and to give you access, and the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 and the state rules require the record to be kept for a defined period.
tips.sources: Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Charter of Patients' Rights. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Ask for a certified copy, not a photograph of a screen, and check that every page carries the hospital's name and the date. Leave the originals in the hospital's custody and keep your copy at home; do not hand your only copy to an agent. For a chronic condition keep one folder in date order and a single page listing the medicines, the doses and the last results. If the hospital says the record is not ready, ask for that in writing with a date; a refusal is itself worth recording.

tips.title: Emergency care cannot be refused for want of money or ID — the hospital must stabilise first
tips.cost: Emergency stabilisation is provided first; the bill can follow. A government hospital is free or low cost. A private hospital's bill can be recovered later.
tips.inPlainWords: In India, a hospital cannot refuse emergency treatment because the patient cannot pay or has no identity document. The Supreme Court's judgment in Pt. Parmanand Katara v Union of India (1989) requires every hospital to provide immediate emergency care, and the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 and the Charter of Patients' Rights support it. The hospital can recover the cost later, but it must stabilise the patient first.
tips.benefit: The Supreme Court held that every doctor and hospital has a professional obligation to provide emergency care, and that the patient's inability to pay cannot be a reason to refuse. The Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 applies in the states that adopted it. The Charter of Patients' Rights, 2019 lists the right to emergency treatment. A government hospital is funded for emergency care; a private hospital must stabilise and then transfer or bill.
tips.sources: Supreme Court of India, Pt. Parmanand Katara v Union of India (1989). <https://www.sci.gov.in/>; Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Charter of Patients' Rights. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A hospital may transfer a stabilised patient to a facility with the needed specialty. Keep the triage record and the time of arrival. A refusal can be a complaint to the state health department and the consumer commission.

tips.title: A disability assessment should wait until the condition is stable — an early assessment can understate a permanent impairment
tips.cost: The assessment at a government hospital is free or carries a small fee. The cost of an early assessment is a lower rating that is hard to revise.
tips.inPlainWords: In India disability is assessed under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. The Act lists 21 specified disabilities, and the rules made in 2018 set out how a medical authority assesses the percentage of disability and when a person meets the 40% "benchmark disability" threshold. There is no single national waiting period. The medical authority assesses the impairment that remains, so an assessment done while a fracture is still healing or a nerve is still recovering can record less disability than you will have later. Ask the certifying authority when to apply.
tips.benefit: The RPwD Act, 2016 recognises 21 disabilities, including locomotor disability, visual and hearing impairment, intellectual disability, mental illness and multiple disabilities, and provides for a certificate from a medical authority. The 2018 rules prescribe the assessment guidelines and the 40% benchmark for the benefits that attach to benchmark disability. The certificate is issued through the UDID portal and is the basis for reservation, concessions and some social-security benefits. Compensation for a motor accident or a work injury is assessed separately under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 or the employees' compensation law, and the two assessments serve different purposes.
tips.sources: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, UDID. <https://www.swavlambancard.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Do not confuse the three assessments: the RPwD certificate for benefits, the motor accident compensation assessment, and the work-injury assessment under the employees' compensation law. Each uses its own scale and its own authority, and one does not substitute for another. A condition that may improve can be reassessed; ask the certifying authority about the review. Bring the full record, because a missing report is a common reason for a lower rating. A private doctor's letter is not the statutory certificate.

tips.title: After treatment, get a disability certificate and a UDID from the district medical board if an impairment remains
tips.cost: The assessment is free or has a small fee at a government hospital.
tips.inPlainWords: If an injury or illness leaves a lasting impairment, apply for a disability certificate from the district medical board under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. The certificate is linked to a Unique Disability ID (UDID). It is the basis for a reservation, a concession, a scholarship and some social-security benefits. A private doctor's letter is not the statutory certificate.
tips.benefit: The RPwD Act, 2016 lists the recognised disabilities and provides for an assessment by a medical board. The UDID portal issues a card that can be used across states. The certificate supports a reservation in education and employment, a transport concession, and some state allowances. A reassessment is possible if the condition changes. The Act also prohibits discrimination.
tips.sources: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, UDID. <https://www.swavlambancard.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The certificate is not a guarantee of a job; the reservation rules apply to identified posts. A temporary impairment may get a temporary certificate. Keep the medical records for the assessment.

tips.title: Thank the team with a letter or honest feedback, not cash — a cash gift to a doctor is a conduct violation, and for a government doctor a criminal risk
tips.cost: A letter costs nothing. A bribe costs money and can create a criminal record for the person who takes it.
tips.inPlainWords: Offering money to jump a queue or to get a bed does not buy you a right, and it puts the doctor at risk. In India a doctor's conduct is governed by the National Medical Commission's Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations, 2023, and a government doctor is also a public servant under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. Gratitude is not the problem: a letter to the hospital, a note naming the team, or the hospital's patient-feedback form is the right way to say thank you.
tips.benefit: The NMC's 2023 regulations set the professional-conduct rules for registered practitioners, including the standards on gifts, referrals and relationships with patients and industry. The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 applies to a public servant, and a doctor in a government hospital is one; a demand for money for a service that should be free is a matter for the hospital's vigilance officer and the anti-corruption bureau. A private hospital's own code and the consumer law apply to the rest. Feedback through the hospital's grievance cell or the state health department's portal is recorded and can change how a department runs.
tips.sources: National Medical Commission. <https://www.nmc.org.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A gift that is refused is not a personal rejection; the doctor may be required to refuse it. Cash is different from a thank-you letter: the first can end a career and, for a government doctor, attract a criminal case. Do not offer money before treatment either — a bed, a slot or a test is allocated by the hospital's rules, and an offer can be treated as a bribe. If you believe you were asked for money, note the date, the name and the amount, and complain to the hospital's grievance officer or the state health authority; for a government hospital the vigilance officer is the route.

tips.title: For a dental implant, get an itemised quote for every component and check the implant's CDSCO registration — India has no national price cap
tips.cost: The quoted price is rarely the final price: ask for the total for implant, abutment, crown, bone graft, imaging and follow-up. Compare that total, not the headline figure.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no national price cap for a dental implant, and no scheme that fixes the all-in cost. The implant, the abutment, the crown, the bone graft, the imaging and the follow-up are separate items, and a clinic can quote a low price for the screw alone. Ask for a written, itemised quote for the whole treatment, and ask for the brand and the CDSCO licence number of the implant. A dental implant is a medical device, regulated by CDSCO under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017.
tips.benefit: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation regulates medical devices, and a dental implant sold in India should carry a licence that can be checked on CDSCO's portal. The dentist should be registered with the State Dental Council under the Dentists Act, 1948. A government dental college or a district hospital's dental department is usually the cheapest place for the same procedure, though the waiting list is longer. Most health insurance policies exclude cosmetic dental work and may exclude implants; check the policy wording before you assume cover.
tips.sources: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Dental Council of India. <https://dciindia.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A quoted "per implant" price often excludes the abutment, the crown, the bone graft, the CT scan and the follow-up. Ask what happens if the implant fails and what the revision costs. A missing tooth does not always need an implant: a bridge or a removable denture is a legitimate alternative and usually cheaper. Do not choose a clinic on price alone; ask how many of these procedures the dentist does, and look at the infection-control arrangements. Treatment abroad is not a saving if the follow-up happens in another country.

tips.title: If a medicine is out of stock, ask for a generic or a Jan Aushadhi alternative — not a 'negotiated' price
tips.cost: A generic or Jan Aushadhi medicine is usually cheaper than the branded version.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no national insurance-negotiated drug price for every medicine. If a hospital pharmacy is out of stock, ask the doctor for a prescription you can fill at a Jan Aushadhi Kendra, a generic pharmacy or another chemist. Ask for the generic name, not only the brand. A Jan Aushadhi store sells quality generic medicines at a lower price.
tips.benefit: The Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana runs Jan Aushadhi Kendras with generic medicines at a lower price. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority caps the price of scheduled formulations under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. A doctor can prescribe by the generic name, and a pharmacist must dispense the prescribed medicine. A government hospital's pharmacy is usually cheaper than a private one.
tips.sources: Pharmaceuticals & Medical Devices Bureau of India, Jan Aushadhi. <https://janaushadhi.gov.in/>; National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority. <https://www.nppaindia.nic.in/>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A generic must be from a licensed manufacturer; check the batch and the expiry. Do not buy from an unlicensed online seller. A substitution by the pharmacist needs the doctor's consent where the law requires it.

tips.title: For a stable chronic disease, a teleconsultation can renew a prescription — use a registered doctor and a recognised platform
tips.cost: eSanjeevani is free. A private platform charges a consultation fee.
tips.inPlainWords: The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines, 2020 allow a registered medical practitioner to consult and prescribe online, with limits. A first consultation for a serious condition, or a drug on the restricted list, needs an in-person visit. Use eSanjeevani, a hospital's official tele-OPD, or a platform that shows the doctor's registration number. Keep the prescription and the payment record.
tips.benefit: The guidelines set out what a doctor may prescribe in a first teleconsultation and what needs an in-person examination. eSanjeevani, run by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, provides free teleconsultation at many public facilities. A prescription must carry the doctor's registration number and the date. A platform must follow the IT Rules and the data-protection law.
tips.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Telemedicine Practice Guidelines 2020. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; eSanjeevani. <https://esanjeevani.mohfw.gov.in/>; National Medical Commission. <https://www.nmc.org.in/>
tips.caveats: A teleconsultation is not suitable for chest pain, a severe injury or a new neurological symptom; go to an emergency department. A 'prescription' from an unregistered seller is not valid. Do not share an OTP with a platform.

tips.title: Audit the itemised bill line by line, query every charge you do not recognise, and use the consumer and scheme grievance routes
tips.cost: Filing before a consumer commission carries a fee that rises with the claim. A written query at the billing desk costs nothing and resolves most disputes.
tips.inPlainWords: You are entitled to an itemised bill, and to know what you are paying for before you consent to a treatment that your insurance does not cover. If a charge is duplicated, an investigation was not done, or a consumable appears twice, raise it with the hospital's billing or grievance desk while you are still admitted, and keep a written record. If the hospital will not correct it, the routes are the state clinical establishment authority, the consumer commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and, for a scheme patient, the scheme's own grievance channel.
tips.benefit: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers medical services as "service", the position the Supreme Court set in Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995), so a deficient service can be taken to a district, state or national consumer commission. The Charter of Patients' Rights, 2019 sets out the patient's right to information about the cost of treatment. For a PM-JAY patient the hospital is paid a package rate, and a demand for cash on top of the package is a fraud that the State Health Agency and the National Health Authority's anti-fraud system can act on. The National Consumer Helpline (1915) can log a complaint and direct you to the right forum.
tips.sources: Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; National Health Authority, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Charter of Patients' Rights. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A consumer complaint has a limitation period and needs documents: the bill, the discharge summary, the correspondence and the estimate. Keep the original bill; a photograph is not enough. A scheme grievance is about the fund, not about a refund to you, so pursue the hospital's billing desk for your own money at the same time. Ask for the estimate in writing before a non-covered item is used, except in an emergency. At discharge, ask for the final itemised bill and file it with the discharge summary.
